draft.title: Theories and laws
card: Law
A scientific law describes a pattern that is seen every time under the same conditions. It tells us what happens, but not why.
Theory
A scientific theory explains why something happens. It is built on a large body of evidence gathered by many scientists.
For example, a law says that a dropped ball always falls towards the ground. The theory of gravity explains why it falls.
A theory does not become a law when it is proven. Laws and theories do different jobs. Either can change when new evidence appears.
draft.remember: A law describes what happens. A theory explains why. Both can change with new evidence.

a.q: Which statement is a scientific theory rather than a law?
opts: Matter is made of moving particles, which explains smells spreading
Water always boils at a lower temperature on a high mountain
A metal bar always gets longer when it is heated
A rolling ball always slows down on rough ground
a.why: A theory explains why something happens. The statement about moving particles gives a reason for smells spreading. The other three only describe a pattern that happens every time, so they are laws.
a.clue: Look for the statement that gives a reason, not just a pattern.

b.q: Ana says: "A theory is just a guess. When it has enough evidence, it turns into a law." Which reply is correct?
opts: A theory explains why and a law describes what
A theory is a weak idea that becomes a law when proven
A theory cannot change, but a law can change with evidence
A law is more certain than a theory because it is simpler
b.why: Theories and laws do different jobs: a law describes a pattern and a theory explains why. One does not grow into the other. The idea that a theory becomes a law is a common mistake, and it ignores that a theory is built on a large body of evidence.
b.clue: Think about what each one does, not how strong it is.
